families.s: HSE safety management of organisational change
families.t: staff reductions, outsourcing, roles, departments, hazard controls, stress, simultaneous changes, phasing and monitoring
f: Organisations often face pressure for restructuring and staff reductions.
Changes to staffing, contractors, departments, roles and responsibilities can affect control of hazards.
Organisational changes are often analysed less rigorously than plant or process changes.
Poorly conceived or implemented changes can damage safety.
Rapid or continuous change can increase stress and harm health.
Direct and indirect effects of proposed change on hazard control should be identified and assessed.
Major-hazard organisations should apply high reliability to change planning and decision making.
Too many simultaneous changes should be avoided and changes should be phased where possible.
families.g: Staff reductions, outsourcing, roles, departments, hazard controls, stress, simultaneous changes, phasing and monitoring guidance is general organisational and human-factors evidence and does not prove current staffing, competence, behaviour, controls, performance or exact risk at an individual parcel.

families.s: HSE reliability and usability of safety procedures
families.t: instructions, checklists, decision aids, diagrams, incidents, overreliance, user involvement, validation and revision
f: Procedures are agreed safe ways of working and provide instructions and related information.
Job aids can include step-by-step instructions, checklists, decision aids, diagrams and flowcharts.
Inadequate procedure management has contributed to major accidents, injuries and ill health.
Risk can arise from overreliance on procedures, failure to follow them or inadequate procedures.
Procedures should not be the sole defence against human error where stronger controls are practicable.
Users should be involved so procedures reflect the real task and working conditions.
Procedures should be clear, accessible, usable and consistent with equipment and interfaces.
Safety-critical procedures should be validated, controlled, reviewed and updated after change or learning.

families.t: skills, experience, knowledge, risk assessment, managers, practice, unusual work, emergencies, assessment and maintenance
f: Competence is the ability to perform responsibilities and activities to a recognised standard on a regular basis.
It combines skills, experience and knowledge.
Inadequate competence management has contributed to major accidents, injuries and ill health.
Competence assurance should link to safety-critical responsibilities, activities and tasks identified by risk assessment.
Systems should establish and maintain competence for everyone in safety-related work, including managers.
Training is important but is not sufficient on its own.
Practice and consolidation are necessary to develop and retain competence.
Competence systems should cover infrequent, complex, emergency, upset and maintenance conditions.

families.t: site inspections, accident investigations, COMAH reports, competence, failures, procedures, communications, culture, alarms, fatigue and change
f: The toolkit supports HSE inspectors considering human factors during site inspections.
It also supports human-factors consideration in accident investigations.
The toolkit can be used when assessing company documents such as COMAH safety reports.
Core topics include competence assurance.
Core topics include accident investigation, identifying human failures and procedure usability.
Common topics include emergency response, maintenance error, safety-critical communication and safety culture.
Specific topics include alarm handling, fatigue risk and organisational change.
The toolkit provides structured prompts but does not replace evidence about the actual site, task or organisation.

families.t: human failures, staffing, communications, design, culture, maintenance, competence, fatigue, change and procedures
f: HSE's common-risks index groups human-factors topics into a structured set.
The managing-human-failures group includes overview, human errors and investigation.
The staffing group includes staffing levels, workload, supervision and contractors.
The safety-critical communication group includes communication overview, shift handover and permit-to-work.
The design group includes control rooms, interfaces, alarms and the physical work environment.
The organisational-culture group includes culture, behavioural safety and learning organisations.
The maintenance, inspection and testing group includes MIT management, maintenance error and intelligent-customer capability.
The wider taxonomy also links competence, fatigue, organisational change and procedures as related human-factors controls.
